# Mississippi — Commercial UAS Regulatory Summary

**Prepared for:** AEC (surveying, mapping, construction, inspection) UAS program management
**Research date:** August 2, 2026
**Version:** 2.0 (Phase 2 — practical interpretation complete)
**Model / checkpoint:** Objective research model retained from Phase 1; Phase 2 interpretations drafted with OpenAI GPT-5 (Codex; exact checkpoint unavailable)
**Scope note:** This summary covers Mississippi state and state-agency-level UAS authority only. FAA Part 107 is the nationwide operating baseline and is not restated except where a Mississippi source expressly relies on or modifies it. Local (municipal/county) UAS ordinances and tribal UAS considerations are deferred under the current research program and are not researched here, although Mississippi's state/local preemption posture is addressed because it is itself a state-level finding: Mississippi enacted a statewide UAS preemption statute in 2023 (Miss. Code Ann. § 61-21-9), which is a materially different posture than states that have not preempted local UAS ordinances.

> **Process note:** Objective research is retained from the Phase 1 source packet. The four practical-interpretation roles were completed in Phase 2 on 2026-08-02 using OpenAI GPT-5 (Codex; exact checkpoint unavailable).

Each authority below retains its verified objective summary and now includes the four Phase 2 practical-interpretation perspectives. The interpretations are AI-generated operational opinions, not legal advice.

## 1. State UAS Regulatory Overview

Mississippi regulates UAS through a criminal statute targeting critical-infrastructure and correctional-facility surveillance (the Mississippi Unmanned Aircraft Systems Protection Act of 2021, Miss. Code Ann. §§ 97-47-1 to 97-47-9), a separate 2023 statute that both authorizes recreational/commercial UAS operation and preempts most local UAS ordinances (the Uncrewed Aircraft Systems' Rights and Authorities Act, Miss. Code Ann. §§ 61-21-1 to 61-21-11), and a distinctive state-procurement statute requiring domestically manufactured small UAS (and banning Chinese-manufactured UAS) for state and political-subdivision purchases and state-contracted infrastructure-inspection services (Miss. Code Ann. § 31-7-67). Unlike Minnesota, Mississippi has affirmatively preempted local UAS ordinances (subject to enumerated exceptions for government-owned UAS, FAA-enforcement ordinances, generally applicable non-UAS-specific nuisance/trespass ordinances, and property-owner launch/landing control), and does not impose a state-level UAS registration or commercial-operator license beyond what the FAA requires. Substantive UAS restrictions exist for Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks (MDWFP)-managed Wildlife Management Areas (launch/landing prohibition) and state parks (aircraft-operation prohibition absent written Executive Director permission), and for alligator hunting (drone-assisted location/pursuit/take prohibition). No UAS-specific guidance from Mississippi's professional engineering/surveying licensing board, no MDOT Aeronautics Division UAS-specific policy, no gubernatorial executive order, no Attorney General opinion, and no state appellate court decision addressing UAS were located in this pass. A notable and recurring pattern in this research: several UAS-related bills — a 2023 bill (HB 839) that would have created much of the preemption/rights framework that a companion Senate bill (SB 2146) ultimately did enact, and 2024/2025 bills (HB 1370, HB 1494) that would have added UAS-specific language to Mississippi's general trespass statutes and to the licensed-surveyor land-entry statute — were reported in secondary sources in ways that could be mistaken for current law; all of the trespass/surveyor-entry bills specifically died in committee and are NOT currently enacted (see Section 5).

## 2. Statewide UAS Laws and Regulations

### Mississippi Unmanned Aircraft Systems Protection Act of 2021 (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 97-47-1 to 97-47-9)
`Binding statute (criminal) | Current / in force`

**Objective Summary:** Section 97-47-5 makes it an offense to knowingly (a) use a UAS to conduct surveillance of, collect information or data from, or photographically/electronically record a "critical infrastructure" or "correctional facility" without the prior written consent of the owner or owner's designee, or (b) deliver or attempt to deliver contraband by UAS onto correctional-facility property or adjacent property. "Critical infrastructure" is defined narrowly at § 97-47-3(b) as a petroleum refinery or tank farm; an electrical power generation facility supporting the Mississippi power grid; a natural gas processing and terminal facility; a federal or state military installation; or an entity contracted by the Department of Defense or State Military Department to produce defense products — it does **not** extend to water/wastewater, telecommunications, ports, or rail/freight facilities. "Correctional facility" covers state, federal, municipal/county, and youth-detention confinement facilities. Section 97-47-9 makes a violation of (a) a misdemeanor (up to 1 year and/or a $1,000 fine) and a violation of (b) a felony (3-15 years and/or a $25,000 fine). Section 97-47-7 exempts law-enforcement UAS use for any lawful purpose, permits other public agencies/contractors to operate a UAS over such sites only with the facility owner's written consent and FAA-rule compliance, and provides that the chapter does not apply to UAS operating under an FAA Certificate of Waiver or Authorization.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Map the statute's specifically defined critical-infrastructure and correctional-facility boundaries before planning the sensor footprint, and obtain prior written owner or designee consent for covered collection. Keep delivery devices and loose payloads out of correctional-facility missions, with lost-link and emergency procedures designed to prevent entry or delivery onto the facility or adjacent property.
- **Agency Practitioner:** The facility owner or designee should provide a written consent route that identifies the covered site, operator, aircraft, pilots, dates, collection purpose, sensor limits, data recipients, and field contact. Public agencies and contractors should also preserve FAA-compliance evidence and the facility owner's consent rather than treating a project assignment as implicit authorization.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** For correctional-facility work, use configuration control for payload mounts, release mechanisms, return-to-home, and lost-link behavior so the aircraft cannot inadvertently deliver an object onto covered or adjacent property. Procurement should also support geospatial mission boundaries and auditable sensor settings, but those controls do not replace written owner consent.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the signed facility-owner or designee consent, proof of the signer's authority, boundary map, mission and sensor limits, FAA status, and all amendments. Escalate whether a site meets the statute's narrow definitions, whether adjacent property is implicated, or whether a proposed payload could be characterized as contraband delivery before flight.

### Uncrewed Aircraft Systems' Rights and Authorities Act (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 61-21-1 to 61-21-11)
`Binding statute | Current / in force`

**Objective Summary:** Enacted in 2023 (Laws 2023, ch. 306, SB 2146), this chapter authorizes an individual, in compliance with federal law, to operate a UAS recreationally, and an individual or business entity doing business lawfully in Mississippi to operate/use a UAS commercially (§ 61-21-5), without any state registration requirement beyond what federal law requires. Section 61-21-7 makes a person liable for an act or offense committed with the aid of a UAS to the same extent as if performed directly, and confirms a UAS can be the instrumentality of a privacy-rights tort. Section 61-21-9 — Mississippi's preemption provision — bars a political subdivision from enacting or enforcing an ordinance relating to UAS ownership, operation, design, manufacture, testing, maintenance, licensing, registration, certification, airspace, altitude, flight paths, equipment, or pilot/operator/observer qualifications, subject to exceptions permitting a political subdivision to enforce FAA restrictions, regulate its own government-owned/operated UAS, enforce generally applicable (non-UAS-specific) nuisance/voyeurism/harassment/trespass/property-damage ordinances, and regulate UAS launch/landing/pilot-presence on its own property. The Act also protects UAS takeoff/landing for emergency or critical-infrastructure maintenance support, technical-malfunction landings, sworn public-safety-officer operations, and federal-government operations.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Use the state preemption rule to screen UAS-specific local restrictions, but still check generally applicable nuisance, voyeurism, harassment, trespass, and property-damage rules and the public owner's launch, landing, and pilot-location conditions. Record the route, launch and landing rights, emergency or maintenance basis if used, and any non-UAS-specific site restrictions in the flight packet.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Do not describe Mississippi preemption as eliminating all local or property controls; the Act preserves enumerated ordinances and public-property authority and leaves ordinary liability intact. Escalate novel local UAS restrictions, privacy-intensive collection, or reliance on an emergency, malfunction, infrastructure-maintenance, or public-safety landing protection.

### State-Purchased Small UAS — Domestic Manufacturer, Collision-Avoidance, and Country-of-Origin Requirements (Miss. Code Ann. § 31-7-67)
`Binding statute | Current / in force`

**Objective Summary:** Beginning January 1, 2025, all sUAS purchased by the State of Mississippi or any agency/political subdivision must be purchased exclusively from a "domestic manufacturer" (U.S.-incorporated and headquartered, majority American-owned, manufacturing in the U.S.), must possess a collision-avoidance system, and all maintenance/repair/technical services must be performed by a "domestic sUAS company"; all state-contracted infrastructure-inspection services requiring sUAS use must employ domestically manufactured sUAS. Mississippi-based domestic manufacturers and sUAS companies receive a 10% bid preference in Title 31, Chapter 7 procurement, and agencies must solicit at least one bid from a Mississippi-based sUAS manufacturer. An agency may not purchase or operate an sUAS manufactured in the People's Republic of China (including assembly outside China using more than a negligible amount of PRC-origin parts, software, components, or raw materials), subject to a research-institution exemption and a grandfather clause for PRC-manufactured sUAS purchased before January 1, 2025.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** For state-contracted infrastructure inspection, confirm at proposal and aircraft-assignment stages that the consultant-furnished sUAS meets the domestic-manufacturer requirement expressly applied to that service. Keep the public client's purchase and operation rules distinct from an ordinary private project, while treating any incorporated aircraft, collision-avoidance, service, or origin term as a mobilization gate.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Purchasing staff should document domestic-manufacturer status, collision-avoidance capability, required Mississippi bid solicitation and preference, maintenance-provider eligibility, country-of-origin review, and any research or grandfather basis. For infrastructure-inspection contracts, state the aircraft-eligibility requirement expressly and verify the proposed model and configuration before notice to proceed.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Obtain traceable evidence of U.S. incorporation, headquarters, ownership, manufacturing, component and software origin, collision-avoidance capability, and domestic maintenance support before offering a system for covered work. Recheck eligibility at solicitation, award, and deployment, and maintain a replacement plan because a generic 'assembled in the USA' claim does not establish the statute's PRC-content or domestic-manufacturer tests.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Define whether the transaction is a public purchase, public operation, covered state infrastructure-inspection service, grandfathered aircraft, or research-institution use, because the obligations differ. Retain manufacturer and origin attestations, bid records, aircraft configuration, service-provider qualifications, and the contract clause that creates any consultant flow-down.

### Hunter/Angler Harassment Statute — No UAS-Specific Provision Currently Enacted (Miss. Code Ann. § 49-7-147)
`Binding statute | Current / in force (as to its existing, non-UAS text)`

**Objective Summary:** Section 49-7-147 currently prohibits intentionally (a) interfering with or attempting to prevent another's lawful taking of wildlife, (b) attempting to disturb wildlife or affect its behavior with intent to prevent another's lawful taking of it, or (c) harassing a person engaged in lawful taking of wildlife or preparation for such taking; a violation is a Class II violation under Miss. Code Ann. § 49-7-143. The currently codified text contains **no reference to drones, UAS, or unmanned aircraft.** A bill (House Bill 719) proposed amending this section specifically to prohibit using an unmanned system to conduct video surveillance of, or interfere with, a person engaged in lawful hunting or fishing; that amendment was not confirmed enacted, and the current codified section does not contain it.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Screen the mission for active hunting and wildlife sensitivity within Statewide (wherever wild animals are taken or pursued); plan altitude, stand-off distance, route, observers, and abort criteria to avoid pursuit, harassment, surveillance of participants, or assistance to a taking. Document the project's environmental or infrastructure purpose and pause if animals materially react or the flight would disrupt lawful hunting or fishing.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Preserve the legitimate project purpose, active-hunting and fishing screening, route, timing, wildlife response, communications, and any complaint or stop-work action. The current statute is not UAS-specific, so focus the analysis on intentional interference, disturbance, or harassment rather than implying that ordinary project imagery is categorically prohibited.

## 3. State Agency and Facility-Specific UAS Requirements

### MDWFP Wildlife Management Area Rules — UAV Launch/Landing Prohibition (40 Miss. Code R. 2-1.1(GG))
`Binding administrative rule | Current / in force`

**Objective Summary:** The consolidated basic regulations applicable to all Mississippi Wildlife Management Areas (WMAs) provide, at subsection (GG): "Unmanned Aerial Vehicles may not be launched from or landed on MDWFP-Owned Wildlife Management Areas." The rule restricts only launch and landing, not overflight, and exists alongside numerous other WMA use restrictions (target shooting, ORV/vehicle use, hunter-orange requirements, trail-camera identification, etc.) in the same rule, issued under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 39-7-11, 49-1-29, 49-4-4, and 49-5-13.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Plan launch and recovery outside MDWFP-owned WMA land and map the property boundary, alternate landing sites, return-to-home point, and lost-link behavior accordingly. The rule addresses launch and landing rather than overflight, but site access and wildlife or hunting conditions still require separate screening.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Preserve the ownership boundary, launch and landing coordinates, site-access rights, route, return-to-home and emergency-landing plan, and incident log. Do not recast the rule as a general WMA overflight ban, and escalate a mission that lacks a lawful off-property recovery option.

### Alligator Hunting Season Regulations — Drone/UAV Prohibition (40 Miss. Code R. 2-5.2, 2-5.3, 2-5.4)
`Binding administrative rule | Current / in force (see Section 5 on successor-version currency)`

**Objective Summary:** Mississippi's public-waters, private-lands, and Pelahatchie Bay alligator-hunting-season rules each provide that "the use of drones, UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles), or any remotely operated vehicle or vessel to assist in the location, pursuit, and/or take of alligators is prohibited." A violation is a Class III violation under Miss. Code Ann. § 49-7-101. The rules are issued under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 49-1-29, 49-4-4, and 49-7-47.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Screen the mission for active hunting and wildlife sensitivity within Statewide (public waters, private lands, and Pelahatchie Bay alligator-hunting zones); plan altitude, stand-off distance, route, observers, and abort criteria to avoid pursuit, harassment, surveillance of participants, or assistance to a taking. Document the project's environmental or infrastructure purpose and pause if animals materially react or the flight would disrupt lawful hunting or fishing.
- **Agency Practitioner:** N/A — no agency process involved
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Document the legitimate project purpose, alligator-hunting-season and zone screening, route, communications, and any coordination with hunters or land managers. Stop and escalate any request to use imagery or live location data to locate, pursue, or take alligators, even if the requester holds an Alligator Possession Permit.

### General Rules and Regulations for State Parks — Aircraft Operation Restriction (40 Miss. Code R. 6-1.2(W)(18))
`Binding administrative rule | Current / in force`

**Objective Summary:** The rule provides: "Except in an extreme emergency, the operation of aircraft on land or water or the air delivery of any person or thing by parachute, helicopter, hot air balloon or other means, without the written permission of the Executive Director of the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks, is prohibited." The rule text addresses "aircraft" generally rather than naming "drone" or "unmanned aircraft" specifically, but MDWFP's practice treats UAS as covered aircraft requiring the same written special-use-permit process. Issued under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 49-1-29, 49-4-4, and 55-3-33.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat property authorization for State park lands managed by MDWFP statewide as a pre-mobilization gate and obtain conditions that cover launch, landing, route, dates, aircraft, crew, and sensor purpose. Confirm whether the approval is site-wide or location-specific and carry the written authorization and field contact with the crew.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Route the request to MDWFP for written Executive Director permission and identify the state park, operating and recovery areas, dates, aircraft, pilots, purpose, payload, insurance, emergency plan, and field contact. Because the rule supplies no form, fee, or dependable review time, confirm the current submission method and lead time directly rather than inventing a standard process.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Retain the request, written Executive Director permission, proof of scope and conditions, property map, insurance, amendments, and park communications. Confirm in writing that the approval covers the UAS operation and any air delivery or payload activity rather than relying on a client's general access direction.


## 4. Non-Regulatory Context

*The items below are drawn from news and secondary reporting, not primary legal authority. They are provided for situational awareness only and are not part of the verified source register.*

- **Failed trespass/surveillance UAS amendments, Mississippi Legislature (HB 1370, 2024; HB 1494, 2025).** HB 1370 would have added UAS-specific surveillance language to Mississippi's general trespass statutes (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 97-17-85, 97-17-87, 97-17-93, 97-17-97) and to the licensed-surveyor land-entry statute (§ 73-13-103); it passed the House 108-7 on March 12, 2024, but died in Senate Judiciary Division A on April 2, 2024. A nearly identical bill, HB 1494, died in House Judiciary A on February 4, 2025. Neither is current law; AEC firms should not assume UAS-specific trespass liability or surveyor-entry UAS immunity exists in Mississippi beyond the statutes summarized in Sections 2-3 above. [LegiScan HB1370](https://legiscan.com/MS/bill/HB1370/2024); [LegiScan HB1494](https://legiscan.com/MS/bill/HB1494/2025)
- **Failed "Uncrewed Aircraft Systems Rights and Authorities Act" companion bill, Mississippi Legislature (HB 839, 2023).** A House bill containing much of the same preemption/rights framework ultimately enacted via Senate Bill 2146 (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 61-21-1 to 61-21-11) died on the calendar on February 9, 2023; the substance became law only through the separate Senate vehicle, illustrating that bill captions and House passage alone do not confirm enactment. [LegiScan/TrackBill HB839](https://trackbill.com/bill/mississippi-house-bill-839-the-uncrewed-aircraft-systems-rights-and-authorities-act-create/2316643/)
- **Domestic-manufacturer sUAS procurement law, Mississippi Legislature (2023 ch. 460; amended 2024 ch. 498).** Mississippi's state and political-subdivision sUAS procurement law (Miss. Code Ann. § 31-7-67, summarized in Section 2) was amended in 2024 to add the China-manufacture ban effective January 1, 2025, following earlier 2023 legislative attention to a "Mississippi Security Drone Act" concept; AEC firms delivering UAS-based infrastructure-inspection services under Mississippi public contracts should confirm current-list compliance for both the operator's own equipment (where a contract flows the requirement down) and any subcontracted sUAS services.

## 5. Unresolved Operational Questions

- **§ 97-47-5 direct-fetch limitation.** The core offense provision of the UAS Protection Act, § 97-47-5, could not be directly rendered by this pass's web-fetch tool after repeated attempts; its text was instead cross-verified as identical across four independent primary sources (three official Mississippi Legislature bill-drafting texts and a Justia search excerpt). A future pass should attempt a direct, full-page fetch of https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-97/chapter-47/section-97-47-5/ to close this gap formally.
- **Alligator-season rule successor version.** The alligator-hunting drone prohibition (40 Miss. Code R. 2-5.3) was fetched in a version the publisher labels "effective until 7/1/2025." A successor version for the current (2025-2026) season was not independently re-fetched to confirm the drone/UAV prohibition is retained verbatim, though it has been a stable feature across many amendment cycles.
- **MDOT Aeronautics Division.** No public MDOT Aeronautics Division webpage with commercial-UAS-specific guidance, registration, or licensing content (comparable to some other states' DOT aeronautics offices) was located. This should be rechecked periodically in case MDOT publishes such guidance.
- **Hunter-harassment amendment currency (HB 719).** The exact legislative session and final disposition of HB 719 (the bill proposing UAS-specific language for Miss. Code Ann. § 49-7-147) could not be pinned down precisely in this pass; what is confirmed directly is that the current codified § 49-7-147 text contains no UAS-specific language.
- **State UAS procurement/manufacturer restriction scope for private consultants.** Miss. Code Ann. § 31-7-67 binds the state and its agencies/political subdivisions as purchasers and extends the domestic-sUAS requirement to state-contracted infrastructure-inspection services; whether a specific public contract flows this requirement down to a private AEC consultant's own fleet for non-inspection deliverables must be confirmed against the individual contract/RFP.
- **Executive orders, AG opinions, and court decisions.** No Mississippi gubernatorial executive order, Attorney General opinion, or state appellate/supreme court decision addressing UAS was located; this negative finding rests on targeted rather than exhaustive historical searches and should be rechecked in a future currency pass.

Code Ann. § 61-21-5 authorizes an individual, in compliance with federal law, to operate a UAS recreationally, and an individual or business entity doing business lawfully in the state to operate/use a UAS commercially, and provides that a UAS owner is not required to register the aircraft beyond what federal law requires. § 61-21-7 provides that a person is liable for an act or offense committed with the aid of a UAS if the conduct would have given rise to civil or criminal liability had it been performed directly, and that a UAS can be the instrumentality of a privacy-rights tort. § 61-21-9 (the preemption provision) bars a political subdivision from enacting or enforcing an ordinance relating to UAS ownership, operation, design, manufacture, testing, maintenance, licensing, registration, certification, airspace, altitude, flight paths, equipment, or pilot/operator/observer qualifications, subject to exceptions allowing a political subdivision to: enforce FAA restrictions; regulate its own government-owned/operated UAS; enforce generally applicable (non-UAS-specific) nuisance, voyeurism, harassment, trespass, reckless-endangerment, or property-damage ordinances; and regulate UAS launch/landing/pilot-presence on political-subdivision-owned property. § 61-21-9(3) separately clarifies the Act does not prohibit UAS takeoff/landing for emergency or critical-infrastructure maintenance support, technical-malfunction landings, sworn public-safety-officer operations, or federal-government operations.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Use the state preemption rule to screen UAS-specific local restrictions, but still check generally applicable nuisance, voyeurism, harassment, trespass, and property-damage rules and the public owner's launch, landing, and pilot-location conditions. Record the route, launch and landing rights, emergency or maintenance basis if used, and any non-UAS-specific site restrictions in the flight packet.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Do not describe Mississippi preemption as eliminating all local or property controls; the Act preserves enumerated ordinances and public-property authority and leaves ordinary liability intact. Escalate novel local UAS restrictions, privacy-intensive collection, or reliance on an emergency, malfunction, infrastructure-maintenance, or public-safety landing protection.
records.verification_status: Chapter listing plus §§ 61-21-5 and 61-21-9 fetched and read in full directly from law.justia.com (official Mississippi Code text); enactment vehicle (2023 SB 2146, ch. 306) confirmed via the codified History note.
records.notes: Two subsequent bills (2024 HB 1370, passed House 108-7 but died in Senate Judiciary Division A on 2024-04-02; 2025 HB 1494, died in House Judiciary A on 2025-02-04) would have added language to § 61-21-5 conditioning recreational operation on not otherwise violating state law and would have added UAS-specific surveillance language to the general trespass statutes (Miss. Code Ann. §§ 97-17-85, 97-17-87, 97-17-93, 97-17-97) and to the licensed-surveyor land-entry statute (§ 73-13-103). NEITHER BILL WAS ENACTED; the general trespass statutes and § 73-13-103 currently contain NO UAS-specific language. This is flagged because secondary sources and even legislative bill captions can create a false impression that these amendments are current law — they are not. See Non-Regulatory Context in the printable summary.

records.issuing_authority: Mississippi Legislature; state public-procurement framework administered under Title 31, Chapter 7
records.source_title: State-Purchased Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems — Domestic Manufacturer, Collision-Avoidance, and Country-of-Origin Requirements
records.effective_date: 2023-07-01 (Laws, 2023, ch. 460, § 1); amended by Laws, 2024, ch. 498, § 2, eff. 2024-07-01; substantive domestic-manufacturer/China-ban provisions effective 2025-01-01
records.uas_topic: State UAS procurement, manufacturer, and country-of-origin restriction
records.regulated_party: State of Mississippi and its agencies and political subdivisions (as purchasers); domestic manufacturers and domestic sUAS maintenance/repair companies (as bid-preference beneficiaries)
records.regulated_activity: Purchasing, operating, maintaining, or repairing a small UAS ('sUAS') on behalf of the state or a political subdivision; contracting for state infrastructure-inspection services requiring sUAS use
records.requirement_type: Domestic-sourcing mandate; China-manufacture ban (with grandfather exception); in-state bid preference
records.permit_or_approval_required: Not applicable in the permit sense — this is a procurement sourcing/eligibility requirement, not an approval process
records.public_agency_only: Yes — applies to the State of Mississippi and its agencies and political subdivisions as purchasers, not directly to a private AEC consultant's own equipment (see notes on contract flow-down)
records.commercial_operator_relevance: Indirect — governs what the state/political subdivisions may purchase and what a state-contracted infrastructure-inspection sUAS provider must use, rather than private commercial operation generally
records.aec_relevance: Yes — directly relevant to any AEC firm bidding on or delivering Mississippi public-agency UAS infrastructure-inspection work, and to any firm selling or maintaining sUAS to Mississippi public entities
records.summary: Miss. Code Ann. § 31-7-67(2) requires that, beginning January 1, 2025, all sUAS purchased by the State of Mississippi or any agency/political subdivision be purchased exclusively from a 'domestic manufacturer' (U.S.-incorporated and headquartered, majority American-owned, manufacturing in the U.S.), possess a collision-avoidance system, and have all maintenance/repair/technical services performed by a 'domestic sUAS company'; it further requires that all state-contracted infrastructure-inspection services requiring sUAS use employ domestically manufactured sUAS. Subsection (3) grants domestic Mississippi-based manufacturers and sUAS companies a 10% bid preference over non-Mississippi competitors in Title 31, Chapter 7 procurement, and requires agencies to solicit at least one bid from a Mississippi-based sUAS manufacturer. Subsection (4) bars an agency from purchasing or operating an sUAS manufactured in the People's Republic of China, defined to include assembly outside China using more than a negligible amount of PRC-origin parts, software, components, or raw materials. Subsection (5) exempts a state institution of higher learning with a federally designated research center conducting sUAS research, and subsection (6) grandfathers PRC-manufactured sUAS purchased before January 1, 2025.
records.practical_interpretation_aec_expert: For state-contracted infrastructure inspection, confirm at proposal and aircraft-assignment stages that the consultant-furnished sUAS meets the domestic-manufacturer requirement expressly applied to that service. Keep the public client's purchase and operation rules distinct from an ordinary private project, while treating any incorporated aircraft, collision-avoidance, service, or origin term as a mobilization gate.
records.practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Purchasing staff should document domestic-manufacturer status, collision-avoidance capability, required Mississippi bid solicitation and preference, maintenance-provider eligibility, country-of-origin review, and any research or grandfather basis. For infrastructure-inspection contracts, state the aircraft-eligibility requirement expressly and verify the proposed model and configuration before notice to proceed.
records.practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Obtain traceable evidence of U.S. incorporation, headquarters, ownership, manufacturing, component and software origin, collision-avoidance capability, and domestic maintenance support before offering a system for covered work. Recheck eligibility at solicitation, award, and deployment, and maintain a replacement plan because a generic 'assembled in the USA' claim does not establish the statute's PRC-content or domestic-manufacturer tests.
records.practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Define whether the transaction is a public purchase, public operation, covered state infrastructure-inspection service, grandfathered aircraft, or research-institution use, because the obligations differ. Retain manufacturer and origin attestations, bid records, aircraft configuration, service-provider qualifications, and the contract clause that creates any consultant flow-down.
records.verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from law.justia.com (official Mississippi Code text), including the History note confirming the 2023 enactment and 2024 amendment.
records.notes: This statute binds the state and its agencies/political subdivisions as purchasers and, for infrastructure-inspection services, extends the domestic-sUAS requirement to the contracted service itself; it does not, on its face, restrict equipment a private AEC firm may own or use for non-state work. Whether a specific public contract's terms flow this requirement down to a consultant's own fleet must be confirmed against the individual contract/RFP, consistent with the project's procurement-interpretation guardrails.

The rule addresses launch and landing rather than overflight, but site access and wildlife or hunting conditions still require separate screening.

Code Ann. § 49-7-147 currently prohibits intentionally (a) interfering with or attempting to prevent another's lawful taking of wildlife, (b) attempting to disturb wildlife or affect its behavior with intent to prevent another's lawful taking of it, or (c) harassing a person engaged in lawful taking of wildlife or preparation for such taking; a violation is a Class II violation under Miss. A bill (House Bill 719, apparently introduced in an earlier session) proposed amending this section specifically to prohibit using an unmanned system to conduct video surveillance of, or interfere with, a person engaged in lawful hunting or fishing; that amendment was not confirmed enacted, and the current codified section (verified directly) does not contain it.
